⚡🇱🇧🇮🇱 20 years ago, on August 5, 2006, a Lebanese Army adjutant proved that Lebanon's power relies on the equation:
army–people–resistance.
On that day, Israeli naval commandos from Shayetet 13 carried out a nighttime raid on an apartment building in the northern outskirts of Tyre, Lebanon, during the 2006 Lebanon War. The target was allegedly to capture the official in charge of Hezbollah's missile unit.
Ehud Olmert, former Prime Minister of Israel, stated: "I was directly monitoring the landing operation of the paratrooper unit. Just as the operation was about to succeed without anyone noticing, a Lebanese soldier emerged and began firing toward the helicopter. Afterward, he discovered one of our groups, engaged them, and fell in the confrontation just dozens of meters away. That soldier thwarted the entire operation."
This soldier's name was Nidaa Abu Shaqra, and his bravery alerted Hezbollah to the Israeli operation. This led to the Israeli forces falling into an ambush that left 10 soldiers injured, 1 dead, and roughly 70 stranded .
On November 29, 2018, the Israeli website Walla published previously unseen footage showing the army rescuing its personnel after its forces failed to achieve the mission's objective. The footage showed Israeli airborne personnel rescuing 92 fighters returning from the operation.

🌏 🇮🇷 How Iran is expanding its geopolitical contest with the US and Israel beyond Middle East
Iran is not sitting on the sidelines as Gulf states, Israel and their Western allies extend their influence across Africa, Latin America and Asia – the Islamic Republic is playing its own geopolitical game.
Africa
Iran is accelerating its African outreach: after decades of ties, it made the continent a foreign policy priority in 2024 and convened three Iran-Africa summits between 2023 and 2025, attracting around 40 countries.
🔴 Northern Africa
Alongside Algeria, Iran seeks to counter[ growing US-Israeli influence in Morocco](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73024), opposing Rabat’s entry into the Abraham Accords and rejecting [its claims over Western Sahara.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73083) Reports have also pointed to Iranian support for the Polisario Front, the movement seeking independence for Western Sahara through the self-declared Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR)
🔴 Eastern Africa
Iran has reportedly backed President Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), including via the supply of Mohajer-6 drones between December 2023 and January 2024. Notably, the SAF also enjoys Saudi support, while its rival, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), is backed by the UAE – deeply allied with Israel
After reviving ties with Kenya, Uganda and Zimbabwe in 2023, Iran formalized its long-standing military technical relationship with Ethiopia through a 2025 security and intelligence-sharing deal. Even as Ethiopia works with the UAE, it has[ kept its partnership with Iran on a separate track](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72095)
🔴 Sahel
As Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad curtailed Western military presence between 2022 and 2025, Iran moved to expand its footprint in the Sahel through offers of military cooperation, energy and scientific assistance. Iran's deepening ties with Niger, formalized through 2025 security and cooperation pacts, rattled the US as it lost its military foothold in the African country in 2024.
Latin America
As the Trump administration and Israel move to curb pro-independence governments in Latin America [through overt pressure and alleged electoral fraud](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71363), Iran's relations with Venezuela, Argentina and Bolivia have become strained. Nonetheless, it still maintains close ties with Brazil, Nicaragua and Cuba. Iran's Latin American pivot is driven by [resistance to US pressure and the pursuit of multipolarity](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/69825)
Asia
🔴 China serves as Iran's primary economic lifeline, purchasing the vast majority of its oil exports, while India is involved in its major infrastructure projects such as the [Chabahar Port and the International North-South Transport Corridor ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/66600)
🔴 Iran and North Korea maintain a decades-long strategic partnership rooted in their shared resistance to the West
🔴 Iran has also consolidated relations with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, and especially Tajikistan, which it sees [as a brotherly nation.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72150) The five "stans" remain engaged with Iran despite growing [overtures from the EU, Israel, and Turkey](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71609)
Iran is further expanding its global reach through BRICS+ and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), underpinned by comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with both Russia and China.

🇮🇷📍Why Strait of Hormuz is Iran’s equivalent of the US dollar and China’s rare earths
Shipping may soon resume in the strait, but only after the world accepts a new reality: Iran's effective control over the strategic waterway, the New York Times reports.
Iran and Oman are purportedly close to signing a deal to regulate shipping through the Strait of Hormuz:
🌏 vessels heading into the Persian Gulf will transit a channel near Iran
🌏 ships leaving the Gulf will travel on a channel near Oman
🌏 Iran will control inbound shipping and, in effect, outbound shipping as well, since it will oversee traffic and intervene if necessary
🌏 the agreement will impose a “service fee” to cover environmental, security and staffing costs with revenues being divided equally between Iran and Oman
🌏 from now on, Iran will wield strategic leverage over the strait in a way it never did before the Trump administration's intervention
Strait of Hormuz as a counterweight to US dollar weapon
For Iran, the Strait of Hormuz is a strategic asset comparable to the US dollar or[ China's dominance in rare earths](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72149), argues Policy Tensor.
Iran’s strategy would not necessarily involve a blanket closure of the strait. Friendly nations could continue to pass through, while access could be granted to others willing to pay for passage and comply with Iranian conditions.
The Islamic Republic can calibrate the economic pain it inflicts, applying maximum pressure on its adversaries without triggering unnecessary global fallout. By keeping channels for negotiation open, it also preserves the image of a rational and pragmatic actor – one it contrasts with the US and its allies. That is why Iran is unlikely ever to surrender its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
Chess grandmaster
Iran is not just committed to retaining its leverage over the Strait; it has a calculated strategy to protect it and [enjoys escalation dominance in the region](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72799):
♦️ Iran offsets the US threat to annihilate its energy infrastructure by threatening further strikes on oil and gas facilities across the Gulf
♦️ Trump's threat to cut off Iran's power was met with a warning that the Gulf's lights could go out instead – not to mention the[ region's desalination plants](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68598), on which Israel and the Gulf monarchies depend, while Iran does not 
♦️ A prolonged US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz could be countered by[ closing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72095)to unfriendly nations
♦️ Iran responded to US threats against civilians by threatening to kill one US soldier for every civilian casualty, as outlined by Major General Ali Abdollahi
♦️ The timing is also significant: Trump has been boxed in just before the midterm elections that could shape the remainder of his second term
Iran's grand design
Some experts argue that Iran is exploiting the moment asymmetrically to emerge as a new global power: controlling a strategic maritime chokepoint, projecting influence across the region, and deepening geopolitical ties beyond it – from Africa to Latin America.

🇸🇾🇮🇱 As Israel eats Syria alive, Sharaa clings to peace promises
 
Israeli forces launched a new incursion into the southwestern Syrian province of Quneitra on Sunday, establishing a checkpoint along a road linking the villages of al-Hiran and al-Rafid.
A day earlier, Israeli troops carried out a similar operation in the village of al-Ajraf in Quneitra’s north, setting up a checkpoint, erecting a surveillance camera and leaving.
Also Saturday, the IDF moved into the Wadi al-Raqad area in Dara’a, creating a checkpoint on a local bridge and searching a residential home. In neighboring Maariya and Al-Aarda, troops set up another checkpoint, searched homes, stopped residents from cultivating their land, distributed leaflets warning them not to obstruct their activities, and damaged an electrical transformer, cutting power to one of the villages.
 
The weekend’s incidents are part of a well-established pattern going back to late 2024. After the collapse of the Assad government, Israel launched [a ground invasion](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/64690):
➡️ capturing up to 350 sq km beyond already occupied areas of the Golan Heights
➡️seizing Mount Hermon – putting Israel within artillery striking range of Damascus
➡️ advancing 12km deep into the Quneitra countryside, establishing forward bases, laying mines and conducting raids
➡️seizing control of the trilateral border area where Israel, Syria and Jordan meet, taking over Al-Wehda Dam, a vital local cross-border water lifeline providing drinking and agricultural irrigation water to local communities
➡️ preemptively wiping out 70-80% of Baathist Syria’s military capabilities, including its air defenses, Navy, Air Force, and long-range ballistic and cruise missiles, plus electricity, water and IT infrastructure
[Terrorist-turned president Ahmed al-Sharaa’s](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73035) responded by making fresh promises last week to ink a security deal with Israel that he says could flower into a comprehensive peace agreement.
He’d better hurry and reach a deal, or Tel Aviv might ramp up its ‘Greater Israel’ appetites and leave nothing of Syria but a Bantustan Damascus governorate. But knowing Sharaa’s [allegiances and nature](https://t.me/c/3955555543/1120), he’d probably be content with that too, so long as there were still [minority communities](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72833) to terrorize.
